entities.name: Titus Tarquinius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titus Tarquinius, one of the sons of Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the seventh and last king of Rome, was a central figure in the tumultuous transition from the Roman monarchy to the early Republic, a period spanning the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE. While ancient historians like Livy and Fabius Pictor identify him as the eldest son, Dionysius of Halicarnassus presents a differing account. Regardless of his precise birth order, Titus's significance stems from his active and relentless efforts to restore his family to the Roman throne following their expulsion in 509 BCE, making him a formidable antagonist to the nascent republican government and a catalyst for its consolidation.

Following the overthrow of the Tarquinian monarchy, Titus Tarquinius, alongside his father and brother Sextus, sought refuge with various Latin allies. His most notable involvement came in the critical Battle of Lake Regillus, conventionally dated to 498 BCE (though some scholars place it around 496 BCE). In this decisive conflict, Titus fought alongside his brother-in-law, Octavius Mamilius, the dictator of Tusculum, and a significant contingent of Latin League forces. He reportedly engaged in a fierce duel with the Roman dictator Aulus Postumius Albus Regillensis, and later, according to Livy, was wounded by the Roman consul Spurius Larcius. The battle ended in a decisive Roman victory, effectively crushing the Tarquins' hopes of restoration and establishing the supremacy of the young Republic over its Latin neighbors.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Titus Tarquinius's persistent attempts to restore the Roman monarchy, culminating in his death at the Battle of Lake Regillus, were pivotal in solidifying the nascent Roman Republic's anti-monarchical identity and securing its early stability against internal and external threats.
